content: Sexual violence refers to any act, including trafficking or other actions, directed against an individual’s sexuality through coercion, regardless of the relationship between the perpetrator and the victim, and can occur in any setting, such as at home or in the workplace. Sexual assault, a subset of sexual violence, typically involves the use of physical or other forms of force to achieve or attempt sexual penetration. This includes rape, which is defined as the physically forced or otherwise coerced penetration of the vulva or anus with a penis, other body parts, or objects. Legal definitions of rape may vary and, in some cases, include oral penetration. Routine inquiry refers to the practice of investigating intimate partner violence without implementing a full public health screening program. It may also involve routinely asking women about abuse in healthcare settings, though not necessarily all women. Screening, or universal screening, involves large-scale assessments of entire population groups without selecting specific subgroups. Shared decision-making occurs when clinicians and patients collaborate to make healthcare decisions using the best available evidence. Patients are encouraged to consider their options, weigh the potential benefits and harms, communicate their preferences, and choose the course of action that aligns with their values and needs. A shelter, also known as a safe house or refuge, is typically a secure location where women can escape abusive partners. These are often operated by non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and were first established as a response to partner violence by the feminist movement in high-income countries during the 1970s. Shelters may also include churches, community groups, or other settings that provide a safe haven for women. Support, as defined in these guidelines, encompasses a range of services, including legal, housing, and financial advice; access to community resources such as shelters; emergency housing; psychological interventions; and safety planning advice. Violence against women is a broad term defined by the United Nations as any act of gender-based violence that results in, or is likely to result in, physical, sexual, or mental harm or suffering to women. This includes threats, coercion, or arbitrary deprivation of liberty, whether occurring in public or private life. It encompasses various forms of violence, such as intimate partner violence, non-partner sexual violence, trafficking, and harmful practices like female genital mutilation. Women who have experienced violence often seek healthcare for their injuries, even if they do not disclose the associated abuse. Healthcare providers are frequently the first professionals to encounter survivors of intimate partner violence or sexual assault. Abused women tend to use healthcare services more than non-abused women and identify healthcare providers as the professionals they trust most to disclose abuse. These guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations to healthcare providers on how to respond appropriately to intimate partner violence and sexual violence against women. This includes clinical interventions and emotional support. The guidelines also seek to raise awareness among healthcare providers and policymakers about violence against women and the need for an appropriate health-sector response. The guidelines are based on systematic reviews of evidence related to identifying and providing clinical care for intimate partner violence and sexual assault, as well as training healthcare providers. They offer standards that can serve as the foundation for national guidelines and for integrating these issues into healthcare provider education. They also aim to inform healthcare providers about the care of women experiencing sexual assault and intimate partner violence. Although men can also be victims of partner violence and sexual assault, these guidelines focus on women, as they experience higher rates of sexual violence, more severe physical violence, and greater coercive control from male partners. However, some advice may also be relevant for violence against women by family members other than intimate partners, partner abuse of men, and sexual assault of men. The target audience for these guidelines includes healthcare providers, who are uniquely positioned to address the health and psychosocial needs of women who have experienced violence. Healthcare professionals can assist by facilitating disclosure, offering support and referrals, providing appropriate medical services and follow-up care, and gathering forensic evidence, particularly in cases of sexual violence. The guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for healthcare providers on appropriate care, including clinical interventions and emotional support, for women suffering from intimate partner violence and sexual violence. They also aim to increase awareness among healthcare providers and policymakers about violence against women, encourage evidence-informed health-sector responses, and improve the capacity of healthcare providers and multidisciplinary teams. The guidelines include a service-delivery and programmatic guidance component for those responsible for developing, funding, and implementing programs to address violence against women. The level of available resources, including other support services, must be considered when implementing the recommendations. The World Health Organization (WHO) will collaborate with ministries of health, NGOs, and other United Nations agencies to disseminate these guidelines and support their adaptation and implementation in member states. The development of these guidelines involved identifying clinical and policy-related questions, retrieving up-to-date evidence, assessing and synthesizing the evidence, formulating recommendations with input from a wide range of stakeholders, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and updating. The evidence was synthesized using the GRADE methodology for clinical interventions, and recommendations were developed with input from a diverse group of academics, clinicians, policymakers, and advocates. The recommendations consider the evidence, the balance between benefits and harms, women’s preferences and human rights, and cost implications in different countries and communities. For clinical interventions, the quality of evidence was graded as very low, low, moderate, or high using GRADE methodology. Where no direct evidence was available, recommendations were based on extrapolated evidence from other populations. Recommendations on healthcare policy and provision, as well as mandatory reporting, were considered best practices or addressed human rights. Relevant literature was systematically reviewed and summarized qualitatively, but GRADE was not used to assess the evidence. When no evidence was identified, this was noted in the summary. Recommendations were classified as strong or conditional based on the generalizability of benefits across settings, women’s needs and preferences, and the resources required. To ensure clarity, the Guideline Development Group provided additional remarks below the recommendations. Input from peer reviewers and stakeholders, including those working directly with survivors, helped refine the recommendations. Knowledge gaps requiring primary research were identified, leading to the development of a list of critical research questions.
